html:
Ravenna is a city in north-east Italy, near the Adriatic coast, that was the capital of the Western Roman Empire in its last decades and then of the Ostrogoths and of Byzantine Italy. Its churches hold the finest early Christian mosaics in the world.

Augustus based a fleet at its nearby port of Classe. In 402 the emperor Honorius moved his court there from Milan, because marshes and the sea made it easy to defend and easy to escape from by ship. His sister Galla Placidia ruled the West from Ravenna for her young son and left the small, star-vaulted mausoleum named after her. In 476 the general Odoacer, at Ravenna, deposed the last western emperor.

Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, took Ravenna in 493 and ruled Italy from it. He built churches for his Arian Christians and a mausoleum roofed with a single huge stone. In 540 Belisarius took the city for Justinian during the Gothic War. The church of San Vitale, finished in 547, shows Justinian and Theodora in mosaic.

Ravenna stayed the seat of Byzantine rule in Italy, the exarchate, until the Lombards took it in 751. Its harbour silted up, and the city sank into a quiet provincial town. The poet Dante died there in exile in 1321 and is buried there.
